desc:
Given two strings haystack and needle, return the smallest index i such that needle appears in haystack starting at position i. If needle does not occur in haystack, return -1.

For example, needle = "aba" first occurs in haystack = "ccababa" at index 2, while needle = "abc" does not occur in "ababab", so the answer is -1.

Implement the search yourself; a solution that runs in O(n + m) time is possible.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
needle may be longer than haystack, in which case the answer is -1
hints: Trying every start position and comparing character by character works, but it can take O(n · m) time on strings like "aaaa...a".

When a partial match fails, the characters you already matched tell you which later start positions are still possible. Precompute, for every prefix of the needle, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.

Build that table (the KMP failure function) for needle, then scan haystack once while keeping the current matched length; on a mismatch fall back with the table instead of moving the haystack pointer backwards.
editorial: The naive method aligns the needle at each position and compares until a mismatch. On inputs such as a haystack of 20,000 letters a and a needle of 10,000 as followed by a b, it repeats almost the whole comparison at every shift, which is O(n · m).

The Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm removes that waste. For each prefix of the needle, pi[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of needle[0..i] that is also its suffix. While scanning the haystack, keep k, the number of needle characters currently matched. On a mismatch, set k = pi[k-1] until the characters agree or k is zero; on a match, increase k. When k reaches the needle length the match started at i - m + 1.

Every step either increases k by one or decreases it, and k never goes below zero, so the total number of fallback steps is bounded by the number of increases. Building the table and scanning together take O(n + m) time and O(m) space.
